lesson_title: The Year the Wall Went Up
hook_text: In 1948, a party won an election with fewer votes than its rival, and then it changed every South African's life.
clip_script: May 1948. An election where almost only white people could vote. The National Party promised apartheid. Separateness. It got fewer votes than the United Party, but it won more seats, and it took power. Then the laws came, one after another. 1949: no marriage across the colour line. 1950: every person labelled by race. Every town divided into group areas. 1952: a pass book that black people had to carry everywhere. 1953: separate beaches, buses and benches, and they did not have to be equal. Separate, poorer schools for black children. A label on your identity document decided where you could live, learn, work, love and whether you could vote. This was apartheid. And from day one, people pushed back.
visual_style: Archive photos of 1948 election posters; D.F. Malan at a podium; a typewriter stamping race classifications; a 'Whites only' bench; a pass book being checked by police; children in an overcrowded classroom; protesters with placards.
pacing: A quick drumbeat of laws and dates, slowing at the final line.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to learn how the National Party built apartheid law by law.
